body.text: Most homeowners don't think much about their deck until something is visibly wrong, a soft board underfoot, peeling stain along a railing, or a section that just looks tired next to the rest of the yard. By the time it's obvious, the underlying problem has usually been developing quietly for a season or two already. Catching these signs early is routinely the difference between a $1,200 restoration and a $15,000 rebuild. Here are the five warning signs worth checking every spring, in roughly the order they tend to appear.
1. The wood has turned grey or silver

Natural wood doesn't grey purely from age, it greys because UV radiation is breaking down lignin, the structural compound that binds wood fibres together. Once the surface fibres degrade, the wood becomes rougher, more porous and considerably more susceptible to absorbing moisture and hosting mold. A lightly grey, freshly weathered deck usually restores well with a deep clean and quality stain alone. A deeply weathered, silver-grey deck may need more aggressive cleaning and some surface sanding to bring the grain back. Either condition is restorable in the large majority of cases, but only if the degradation is caught before it reaches the structural level of the board.
2. Water soaks in instead of beading

This is the fastest and most reliable test for whether a deck's stain still has protective life left in it. Splash a cup of water on the deck surface. If it beads up and sits on the wood for several seconds before slowly absorbing, the stain is still working. If it soaks straight in and darkens the wood within seconds, the water-repelling protection is gone. An unprotected deck absorbs moisture every time it rains, and that moisture is exactly what drives mold growth, freeze-thaw damage and, eventually, rot. Catching this sign early means a routine restain. Catching it late tends to mean repairs, or worse.
3. Mold, algae or black staining on the surface

Black streaks, green patches or fuzzy growth on deck boards signal that moisture is consistently sitting in or on the wood. This isn't purely a visual problem, mold and algae produce enzymes and acids that actively break down wood fibres over time. A professionally cleaned deck with fresh stain eliminates the mold and inhibits regrowth going forward, but left untreated, the decay clock keeps ticking. Mold also creates a real slip hazard on wet days, particularly on stairs and railing surfaces where footing already matters most. North-facing or heavily shaded decks are the most vulnerable to this sign, so check those areas more frequently than sun-exposed sections.
4. Boards are soft, spongy or show visible rot

Walk every board on the deck and pay attention to how much each one flexes. Minor flex at the midspan of a longer board is usually normal for the span. Boards that feel distinctly spongy underfoot, or that flex dramatically under your weight, may have compromised structural capacity. Probe any suspected area with a flathead screwdriver: if it sinks in easily, the board is rotted and needs replacing. Rot spreads, a rotted board pressed against a healthy one will transfer moisture and infect the sound wood over time. Replace rotted boards promptly, treat the surrounding area, and seal everything before the problem has a chance to spread further.
5. The stain is peeling, cracking or bubbling

This is the most urgent of the five signs and demands prompt attention. Peeling or bubbling stain means the protective coating has failed completely and moisture has worked its way between the finish and the wood surface. This most often happens with film-forming stains, solid stains, paints and some deck paints, that either weren't applied to fully dried wood or have simply aged past their service life. The critical point here is that you cannot stain over a peeling deck. Any new product applied on top of a failing finish will fail at roughly the same rate, which means the existing coating has to be fully stripped or sanded back to bare wood before recoating, otherwise the money spent on new stain is largely wasted.

If more than one of these signs shows up at the same time, particularly water soaking in alongside greying or mold, that's a strong signal the deck is due for a full professional restoration rather than a spot treatment.
Why catching these early saves real money

Each of these five signs represents a progression, from a cosmetic UV issue through to full structural compromise, and the cost of addressing them rises sharply the later you catch them. Restoring a deck that's simply greying and no longer beading water is a routine job, generally in the $950 to $1,350 range including prep. Wait until boards are rotting or the stain is fully peeling, and the same deck can require board replacement, more extensive sanding and repair work layered on top of the standard restoration, pushing costs well beyond that range. Left long enough, structural issues in the frame itself can turn a restoration into a partial or full rebuild costing many times more. A spring check that takes twenty minutes is consistently the cheapest deck maintenance decision a homeowner can make. See /how-often-should-you-restain-your-deck for typical timelines by stain type, and /how-to-save-money-restore-dont-replace for a deeper look at when restoration versus replacement makes sense.
What to do once you spot one of these signs

The right response depends on how far along the sign is. Greying alone, with water still beading reasonably well, can often wait for the next planned maintenance cycle. Water soaking straight in, or the first appearance of mold, generally means booking a restoration within the season rather than waiting another year. Soft boards or peeling stain should move to the top of the list, since both tend to worsen through the next round of Ontario weather rather than staying stable. faq.q: Is a grey, weathered deck always a sign of serious damage?
faq.a: No. Grey wood is UV breaking down surface lignin, which is a cosmetic and protective issue rather than structural damage. It's restorable in almost every case with a professional deep clean and fresh stain, provided you act before the degradation goes deeper.

faq.q: How do I test whether my deck's stain is still protecting it?
faq.a: Splash a cup of water on the surface. If it beads and sits for a few seconds before absorbing, the stain still has protective life left. If it soaks in immediately and darkens the wood, the barrier has failed and it's time to restain.

faq.q: What does mold or algae on my deck actually mean?
faq.a: It means moisture is consistently sitting in or on the wood, and the mold or algae is actively producing enzymes that break down wood fibres over time. It also creates a slip hazard, particularly on stairs and railings, so it shouldn't be left untreated.

faq.q: How do I know if a soft board needs to be replaced?
faq.a: Probe the suspected area with a flathead screwdriver. If it sinks into the wood easily, the board is rotted and should be replaced promptly, since rot can spread into neighbouring healthy boards through moisture transfer.

faq.q: Can I just apply new stain over peeling or bubbling stain?
faq.a: No. Peeling or bubbling means the existing coating has failed and moisture has gotten underneath it. The old finish must be fully stripped or sanded back to bare wood before any new stain is applied, or the new coat will fail just as quickly.

faq.q: When is the best time of year to check my deck for these signs?
faq.a: Spring, after the last freeze-thaw cycle and before the deck sees heavy summer use, is the ideal window. It gives you time to book a restoration before summer if needed, and lets the deck head into the following winter properly protected.
